sections.overview: Anophthalmus hitleri is a flightless ground beetle known from caves in Slovenia’s Savinja region. Its name, published in 1937, honours Adolf Hitler and has since drawn attention from collectors of Nazi memorabilia.
sections.identification: This eyeless, reddish-brown beetle is 5–5.5 mm long, with long legs; width, height and mass are unreported. Male genitalia aid identification, but no reliable external sex difference or size dimorphism was found.
sections.habitat: Records are concentrated in a few dark, humid caves near Celje, in Slovenia’s Savinja region. A 2012 cave survey recorded eight individuals in one cave, 11–66 m from its entrance and 8–25 m below the surface.
sections.diet: This predatory carabid feeds on tiny cave insects, though detailed prey records remain scarce for this species.
sections.behavior: Like other cave-specialized Anophthalmus, it has lost functional eyesight and flight; the genus runs rapidly over cave floors. In a small cold-tolerance experiment, lower lethal temperature averaged −3 °C in summer and −4.5 °C in winter, with two individuals sampled per season.
sections.reproduction: The 1937 description focuses on adults and male genitalia; species-specific egg or development data were not found.
sections.ecology: It resembles the cave congener Anophthalmus schaumi knirschi, which can be difficult for non-specialists to distinguish; male genital structures help experts tell them apart.
sections.conservation: Slovenia’s 2002 beetle Red List places it in category V, Vulnerable; that dated assessment does not by itself describe current population trends. Its name has drawn attention from Nazi-memorabilia collectors, but the scale and effect of illegal collecting in caves remain uncertain.
